headline: A traveler gave his passcode and his phone erased itself

sources.title: US accuses American of allegedly wiping his phone using a 'duress' password during border search
Border agents can lie to search your phone, but wiping your own data could land you in prison
Traveler Gave CBP A Passcode That Wiped His Phone At Atlanta Airport. Now He Faces Five Years In Prison
Man Prosecuted in First-Ever Phone Duress Password Case (video, FOX 35 Orlando)

chunks.text: Samuel Tunick landed in Atlanta in January 2025 on a [[flight]] from the Dominican Republic. [[Customs]] officers {{pulled him aside}} for a second check and asked him to {{hand over}} the [[passcode]] to his phone. He gave them a code. The screen [[went dark]], [[flashed]] a few times, and the phone [[appeared to]] restart. The code he had typed was a [[duress]] code, and it {{wiped out}} everything on the device.

verbs.correct: To stop someone for extra questioning
verbs.wrong: To check a bag before it boards a plane
verbs.why: Security guards pull aside travelers for a random bag check, and teachers sometimes pull a student aside after class. Customs officers pulled Tunick aside at the Atlanta airport for a second check of his phone.

verbs.correct: To give something to a person in authority
verbs.wrong: To read something out loud to an officer
verbs.why: Drivers hand over their license at a traffic stop, and travelers hand over passports at customs. Tunick handed over his passcode when Customs officers asked for it at the airport.

verbs.correct: To erase everything stored on a device
verbs.wrong: To lock a device until it is unlocked again
verbs.why: A virus can wipe out a hard drive, and a factory reset wipes out every photo and app. Tunick's duress code wiped out his whole phone in seconds, erasing everything he owned.

chunks.text: A duress code is a second passcode that the owner {{sets up}} in advance. When it is typed, it looks exactly like the real one, but [[instead of]] opening the phone it orders a [[factory reset]] and destroys the [[encryption]] keys, so the phone {{starts up}} clean and the old files cannot be read. The feature exists to {{keep out}} anyone who forces the owner to unlock a phone. It is built into GrapheneOS, an [[operating system]] that some people install to replace the software that came with their phone.

verbs.wrong: To type a code very quickly
verbs.why: People set up a spare key with a neighbor, a backup email, or an emergency contact just in case. The phone's owner had set up his duress code long before any officer ever asked for his passcode.

verbs.correct: To begin working from the beginning
verbs.wrong: To send a copy of files to a server
verbs.why: An old car can be slow to start up on a cold morning, and a new laptop starts up in seconds. After the duress code ran, Tunick's phone started up clean, with nothing left on it.

verbs.wrong: To warn the owner about a search
verbs.why: A locked door keeps out strangers, and a strong password keeps out hackers. This duress feature exists to keep out anyone who forces the owner to unlock the phone.

chunks.text: The stop happened in January 2025, but the case only became public in July 2026, and it is being fought in court now. [[Prosecutors]] have charged Tunick with destroying property to stop it being [[seized]], a rarely used law that carries [[up to]] five years in prison. He has pleaded not [[guilty]]. The officers said they were looking for illegal images, but they gave no reason for that [[suspicion]], and Tunick's [[lawyers]] say they had [[nothing to go on]]. They want a [[judge]] to {{throw out}} the [[evidence]] the officers gathered that day, and they argue that the stop would never {{stand up in court}} if the same thing had happened on a street [[rather than]] at an airport.

verbs.wrong: To return property to its owner
verbs.why: A referee can throw out a bad call, and a judge can throw out evidence collected the wrong way. Tunick's lawyers want the judge to throw out everything the officers found on his phone.

verbs.correct: To be accepted as valid by a judge
verbs.wrong: To be argued by a lawyer in person
verbs.why: A weak excuse rarely stands up in court, and neither does evidence gathered without good reason. Tunick's lawyers argue the airport stop would never stand up in court if it had happened on an ordinary street.

chunks.text: The case {{comes down to}} an old question with a new object [[at the center of it]]. Courts have long allowed officers at a border to search a bag without a [[warrant]], and the government says a phone is [[no different]]. Lawyers who work on [[privacy]] say a phone holds a person's whole life, so {{going through}} one is not like opening a suitcase. [[Congress]] has never {{stepped in}} to write a clear rule, and no court has {{sorted out}} the question [[for good]]. Until one does, every traveler who is asked for a passcode is standing in the same [[gray area]] Tunick stood in.

verbs.correct: To depend on one main question
verbs.wrong: To reach a court after many years
verbs.why: A tough decision often comes down to money, and an argument can come down to who spoke first. This case comes down to one question: does a phone deserve the same privacy as a home?

verbs.correct: To examine things one after another
verbs.wrong: To copy every file onto a disk
verbs.why: A detective goes through old case files, and a nurse goes through a patient's chart page by page. Searching a phone means going through years of someone's messages, photos, and private life.

verbs.correct: To get involved in order to act
verbs.wrong: To vote against a proposed law
verbs.why: A manager steps in when a meeting becomes an argument, and a referee steps in to stop a fight. Congress has never stepped in to write a clear rule about phone searches at the border.

verbs.wrong: To pass a brand new law quickly
verbs.why: Neighbors sort out a fence dispute, and a manager sorts out a scheduling conflict before it grows. No court has sorted out whether border agents can demand a passcode from every traveler.

mainIdea.s: A traveler gave border officers a passcode that secretly erased his whole phone using a hidden duress code. He now faces up to five years in prison under a rarely used federal property law.
mainIdea.why: He typed a duress code that wiped the phone on purpose. Prosecutors charged him under a law that carries up to five years in prison.

mainIdea.s: A traveler's phone erased itself by accident when officers handed it back after a routine check. He is now suing the airport for damage to his phone, his belongings, and his travel plans.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the wipe was deliberate, done through a duress code built into the phone. He is the one facing criminal charges, not the airport.

mainIdea.s: Airport officers found a different traveler with an unregistered drone hidden inside his checked bag. Customs took the drone and questioned that traveler for two hours before he flew home again.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a different traveler and a drone found in checked luggage, not the passcode that erased a phone.

lines.text: A traveler landed in Atlanta, and customs officers {{pulled him aside}} for a second check. They asked him to {{hand over}} his phone passcode. He typed a code, the screen flashed, and the phone erased itself.

On purpose. It was a duress code, a second passcode the owner {{sets up}} in advance. It looks like the real one, but it {{wipes out}} everything and destroys the encryption keys. The phone {{starts up}} clean.
[[Wait, that exists?]] Why would phones have that?
The feature exists to {{keep out}} anyone who forces you to unlock your phone. It's built into a special operating system some people install.
Prosecutors charged him with destroying property to stop it being seized, a rarely used law with up to five years in prison. He pleaded not guilty.
What were the officers even looking for?
They said illegal images, but they gave no reason for the suspicion. His lawyers say there was no real evidence, and they want a judge to {{throw out}} what the officers gathered that day.
Can officers really demand your passcode at the border?

[[That's the gray area]]. Courts allow bag searches at borders without a warrant, and the government says a phone is no different. Privacy lawyers say a phone holds your whole life, so {{going through}} one is not like opening a suitcase.
No. Congress never {{stepped in}}, and no court has {{sorted out}} the question [[for good]]. His lawyers argue the stop would never {{stand up in court}} if it had happened on a street.
So the whole case {{comes down to}} one question: is a phone a suitcase?
That's the question a court now has to answer.
